source.title: Rethinking the Role of Normalization and Residual Blocks for Spiking Neural Networks
source.authors: Shin-ichi Ikegawa; Ryuji Saiin; Yoshihide Sawada; N. Natori

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains spiking neural networks, a new setting for the versions’ claims about normalization and residual blocks, and reports classification results. It does not report training classification error or training speed.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy and firing rate, not training error. Its normalization results concern PSP-BN and PSP-LN, not the batch normalization intervention in V6. Table 3 compares post-activation with pre-activation residual blocks in ResNet-106.
record.test_reason: The study uses normalization and residual identity mappings to develop spiking networks, reporting classification accuracy and firing rates. It does not measure depth-dependent training error, training speed, learning-rate tolerance, or another outcome named by V1–V6. Comparing pre-activation and post-activation ResNet-106 models does not establish V3's plain-versus-residual training-error pattern.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that PSP normalization improves classification accuracy while suppressing firing activity, and that combining it with pre-activation residual blocks enables SNNs exceeding 100 layers. These conclusions do not establish the training-error or training-speed claims in V3 or V6.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains spiking neural networks using surrogate gradients and PSP normalization on N-MNIST and F-MNIST; it does not reproduce the claim versions’ ANN recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Residual block type changes reported accuracy in ResNet-106; PSP normalization performance varies with the normalization method, dataset, τs, and λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-activation ResNet-106 achieves 75.4–86.8% accuracy on N-MNIST and 81.6–82.1% on F-MNIST; all corresponding post-activation models achieve 10.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested refractory-period SNNs with PSP normalization, pre-activation residual blocks yield higher classification accuracy than post-activation blocks.

fits_no_version.finding: PSP-BN/LN achieve 97.4/98.2% accuracy on N-MNIST and 88.6/89.1% on F-MNIST, exceeding the other listed methods. Figures 6–7 also report reduced firing activity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Postsynaptic-potential normalization improves classification accuracy and suppresses firing activity in the tested SNNs.

record.problems: The study reports accuracy rather than training error for its depth comparison. It states that only 6K of the training data were randomly sampled each epoch because of computational limits. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted from Tables 2 and 3. Firing-rate curves and totals in Figures 6 and 7 are described qualitatively or shown graphically without recoverable exact values, so they are not entered as numeric rows.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels and size or training-recipe dependencies.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth-dependent training-error degradation in plain networks and its prevention by residual shortcuts; longer training and the initialization exceptions.
Initialization-dependent training speed, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Recovery or divergence relative to an initial stability threshold, curvature changes, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Accuracy gained per training time or iteration, higher learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the extracted V3 limits_scope verdict: an unmeasured part is untested, not a demonstrated limitation. Section 5.1 mentions six-layer models, but the architectures printed in Table 2 contain twelve convolutional layers; retain this source inconsistency when correcting subjects. The supplied text identifies the paper as a preprint and does not substantiate the record's conference attribution.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training error, random or corrupted labels, model size, early stopping, and regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and width differences.

Training error and longer training are not reported; the study uses spiking networks on N-MNIST and F-MNIST rather than batch-normalized ANN models on ImageNet or CIFAR-10. Its comparison is between post-activation and pre-activation residual blocks.
No initialization comparison or signal/gradient propagation measurement.
No learning-rate stability threshold or curvature measurement.
The paper compares PSP normalization methods and no normalization, but does not measure training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and does not test batch normalization as described in this version.

relation.reason: The pre-/post-activation comparison reports classification accuracy at fixed depth; it does not test V3's depth-dependent training-error comparison or V6's training-speed and learning-rate claims.

tranche.reason: Uses normalization and residual identity mappings to develop SNNs; reports method accuracy and firing rates without measuring the training-error, speed, or learning-rate effects specified by V1–V6.

source_check.notes: Table 2 encodes twelve convolutional layers, while Section 5.1 mentions six- and fourteen-convolutional-layer models; preserve this source inconsistency. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; these method-performance rows fit no claim version.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-106 on N-MNIST and F-MNIST with PSP-BN or PSP-LN
reader_labels.reason: Pre-activation results have higher accuracy than post-activation results, but only accuracy is reported, so the stated training-error pattern is not directly established (R1–R8).
